Computation and Language.summary: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

Computation and Language.title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
Computation and Language.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

Computation and Language.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
Computation and Language.summary: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $λ$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

Computation and Language.title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
Computation and Language.summary: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.
authors: Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro. Diego Andrea

Computation and Language.title: Will It Survive? Deciphering the Fate of AI Agent-Authored Code in Open Source
Computation and Language.summary: AI coding agents such as GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex and Devin now open pull requests (PRs) that are merged into open-source projects. Industry reports suggest that AI-assisted code is revised or reverted soon after it is written, which raises the concern that agent code is "disposable". However, little is known about what happens to agent code after it is merged. Knowing how long this code survives, and why it is changed, can help maintainers decide how much review it needs. We performed a survival analysis of the 648,959 lines that 2,794 merged PRs added outside vendored and generated paths in 215 open-source repositories from the AIDev dataset, comparing agent-attributed and human code within the same repositories. Agent-attributed code is not modified sooner than human code. When each PR is weighted equally, agent-attributed lines are modified later (HR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.75, 0.93]). This difference comes from the supervised assistants, mainly Copilot and Codex (HR = 0.76). Code from Devin does not differ from human code over the whole period (HR = 0.95), but among PRs merged after mid-May 2025, code from both the supervised assistants and Devin is modified later. Without PR weighting, the difference is not statistically significant. When agent-attributed code is modified, the intent of the change is similar to that of human code (Cramer's V = 0.080). A file's size and recent changes predict whether agent-attributed code will be modified better than its code tokens do (AUC-ROC 0.78 vs. 0.70), and process features predict when it will be modified only weakly (Macro F1 of 0.31 against 0.25 for a random guess). Our findings suggest that agent code is not disposable, but whether it survives longer than human code depends on the agent, on when the code was merged and on how the comparison is computed.
Computation and Language.comment: This paper has been submitted to a conference and is currently under review

Computation and Language.title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
Computation and Language.summary: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

Computation and Language.title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
Computation and Language.summary:
Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data.
  Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence.
  Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.

Computation and Language.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
Computation and Language.summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.
Computation and Language.comment: 18 pages, 15 tables, 2 figures. Code: https://github.com/Manifestro/kezek ; weights: https://huggingface.co/manifestro/kezek-v1 ; listening examples: https://manifestro.io/models/kezek

Computation and Language.title: SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection
Computation and Language.summary: The easy access to Large Language Models (LLMs) has made AI-generated texts on the web increasingly ubiquitous, making AI-text detection a crucial task. Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.

Computation and Language.title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware
Computation and Language.summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. Nearly every such scheme assumes the receiver can recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly bit for bit. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. We present STEALTH, a scheme built for exactly this setting. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

Computation and Language.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
Computation and Language.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents. The project repository is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauProphet.

Computation and Language.title: CADET: Construction of PCB Routing Instances with Executable Demonstrations
Computation and Language.summary: Printed circuit board (PCB) routing is the stage of physical layout that finds paths connecting the placed pads of each net. Public datasets in this domain are few, and most contain only the final states of routed boards, not demonstrations of the electronic design automation (EDA) engine actions that produce them. To close this gap, we propose CADET (Constructing executAble Demonstrations for Engine-grounded Training), which jointly generates synthetic boards and demonstrations built from EDA engine actions. The resulting RouteDemos provides 100,000 synthetic boards routed with zero design rule violations (DRVs), together with their demonstrations. Their distributions over 17 statistics resemble those of 142 real reference boards. CADET trains a routing policy on these demonstrations with behavior cloning and fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning (RL). On real test boards, the policy raised the rate of complete DRV-free routing from 38.0% to 67.2% over an RL-only baseline. This rate was comparable to that of the open-source autorouter FreeRouting and exceeded those of the other baselines, including GPT-6 Astra. We release the dataset and its generation code as open source at https://github.com/LGAI-Research/CADET.
Computation and Language.comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/LGAI-Research/CADET

Computation and Language.title: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search
Computation and Language.summary: Attributing short LLM-generated texts to a specific source remains challenging for existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding to recover payloads reliably. We propose a codebook-based watermarking scheme that maps an $n$-bit payload to a longer $u$-bit codeword and embeds it during generation through token-level logit biasing. During extraction, the received bit sequence is matched to the nearest codeword in a precomputed secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show that our method achieves near-perfect recovery for 16-24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. Results are weaker on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts, where low-entropy output distributions reduce embedding reliability. We also study a BCH-based variant that avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging. We analyze collision probability, codeword separation, extraction time, tokenization consistency, and text quality, highlighting both the practicality and limitations of codebook-based watermarking for short-form attribution.
Computation and Language.comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security. Code: https://github.com/jaroslawjanas/llmw-codebook

Computation and Language.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
Computation and Language.summary: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.
Computation and Language.comment: 16 pages (excluding references), 20 pages including references; 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to FSEN 2027

Computation and Language.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
Computation and Language.summary: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted to the ICBINB - Failure Modes of AI in Biology Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 15 pages, 6 figures

Computation and Language.title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
Computation and Language.summary: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yuheng98chen/RPD-Unidoc

Computation and Language.title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
Computation and Language.summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.
Computation and Language.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication

Computation and Language.title: DPA: Decentralized Primal Averaging with Quasi-Global Momentum for Highly Heterogeneous Data
Computation and Language.summary: Decentralized training of deep learning models keeps training data local and supports on-device learning over networks. In realistic scenarios, heterogeneity across agents' local data poses an optimization challenge and can severely degrade test accuracy, especially on sparse communication graphs. Building on recent advances in centralized primal averaging, we propose Decentralized Primal Averaging (DPA), a decentralized learning algorithm that combines primal averaging with a local quasi-global momentum buffer. DPA maintains three coupled sequences for optimization, gradient evaluation, and output averaging, while using consecutive mixed iterates to construct a network-aware momentum direction without transmitting an auxiliary tracking variable. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a convergence bound for DPA and identify conditions for linear speedup in the number of agents for sufficiently many iterations. We also introduce DPA-1G, a variant that uses one communication round per iteration and matches the per-iteration communication cost of DSGD-style baselines. Experiments following the GUT decentralized image-classification benchmark show that DPA compares favorably with DSGD, gradient tracking, QG-DSGDm, momentum tracking, and QG-GUTm across datasets, architectures, topologies, and heterogeneity levels, with the largest gains under high heterogeneity on sparse rings. At the same total communication cost, both DPA variants achieve higher mean test accuracy than the best baseline on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-20. Our code is publicly available.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 7 figures. Code available at https://github.com/Diyako754/DPA

Computation and Language.title: MiniOpt: Reasoning to Model and Solve General Optimization Problems with Limited Resources
Computation and Language.summary: Achieving strong optimization generalization across diverse optimization problems while requiring limited training resources remains a challenging problem for optimization-oriented large language models (LLMs). Existing learning-based methods, however, typically require large-scale supervised data, expensive intermediate step verification, and extensive computational resources, while exhibiting limited optimization generalization across diverse optimization structures. In this paper, we propose \textsc{MiniOpt}, a lightweight optimization-specialized LLM trained through a reasoning-to-model-and-solve paradigm and a two-stage training framework with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). MiniOpt encourages structure-oriented optimization learning by reinforcing the completeness of optimization formulations and optimization outcomes. Extensive experiments on eight optimization benchmarks demonstrate that MiniOpt consistently outperforms existing learning-based optimization models while requiring substantially fewer parameters and training data. To further understand optimization generalization, we introduce a complementary parameter-decoupled evaluation protocol that disentangles optimization structure understanding from numerical parameter processing. The results reveal that MiniOpt preserves optimization capability under parameter-decoupled settings significantly better than previous optimization-specialized models, suggesting that its performance gains primarily originate from stronger optimization structure understanding. These findings demonstrate an effective pathway toward efficient and generalizable optimization-specialized LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsiang-1/MiniOpt.

Computation and Language.title: A Modular Framework for ESG Prediction through Domain-Specific Language Modeling and Graph Learning
Computation and Language.summary: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores are increasingly used to evaluate corporate sustainability, supporting investment decisions, ensuring regulatory compliance and assessing risk. However, current ESG evaluations largely rely on proprietary methodologies that often produce inconsistent ratings. This motivates the development of data-driven prediction frameworks. In this paper, we present ESGPred, a modular framework for predicting ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modeling with graph-based learning over a network that models the relationships among the companies being evaluated. In addition to presenting the rationale behind ESGPred and detailing its ESG score prediction process, we show that ESGPred can effectively predict both overall ESG ratings and their individual Environmental, Social, and Governance components. We evaluated ESGPred using a dataset of 5,266 sustainability reports published by 2,134 publicly listed companies between 2020 and 2023. In this evaluation, we used ESG ratings provided by LSEG Data & Analytics as ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrated that integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.

Computation and Language.title: Pointing the Way, Hiding the Destination: Practical Private Dense Retrieval at Scale
Computation and Language.summary: Hosted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search allow users to query valuable provider-held corpora, raising two competing demands: to hide each query and chosen result, yet reveal only the documents that the user is authorized to receive. Existing cryptographic approaches either make this costly by processing the entire corpus for every query, or sacrifice quality for efficiency by scanning a few clusters. We repurpose learned deep hashing as a private filter: a randomized binary code points the provider to a short candidate list, while encrypted reranking and oblivious key transfer protect the precise query and final selection. This shortlist short-circuits full-corpus cryptographic search without sacrificing retrieval quality: with 200-500 candidates, it closely matches full-corpus retrieval across five zero-shot corpora spanning 25K to 5.4M documents. On the full 2.68M-passage NQ corpus over a 10-Gbps link, our protocol only adds 0.38 seconds, or 6.5%, to a 128-token Qwen3-32B RAG pipeline. The released code satisfies directional metric differential privacy (DP) and substantially reduces embedding-inversion and property-inference leakage, demonstrating that a carefully learned shortlist can make private dense retrieval both accurate and practical.

Computation and Language.title: Tree-Based Formalization of Multi-Agent Complementarity in Human-AI Interactions
Computation and Language.summary: Predictive tasks constitute subprocedures within human--AI interactions (HAIs) involving professionals and AI systems. Complementarity occurs when an HAI outperforms a benchmark defined by its constituent agents. Existing formalizations, however, focus on a single human and a single AI, leaving multi-agent interactions insufficiently characterized. We introduce a tree-based mathematical framework for multi-agent complementarity. Ordered agent-role configurations decorate the leaves of rooted planar binary trees and local aggregation rules generate protocol outputs evaluated against either a best-average or a pointwise-min benchmark. We establish four results. First, under linear pooling, every protocol tree provides a bijective coordinate system for the interior of the simplex of global leaf weights. Arbitrary trees with the same ordered leaves admit output- and complementarity-preserving reparameterizations, realized locally through path-independent Tamari rotations. However, HAI constraints can violate admissibility preservation between equivalent protocols. Second, for regression under squared loss, we characterize complementarity through residual correction and derive optimal linear-pooling weights. We also characterize protocol-indifference loci under identical local parameters. Third, selector-based protocols cannot achieve complementarity relative to the pointwise-min benchmark, independently of task and loss. Fourth, in binary classification, HAIs cannot achieve complementarity under endpoint-monotone losses and the pointwise-min benchmark, with an analogous obstruction for multiclass cross-entropy. Numerical illustrations examine the main claims. We provide a mathematical foundation for analyzing multi-agent predictive subprocedures within HAIs, establishing a first step toward understanding how interaction, aggregation, and real-world constraints affect HAI performance.
Computation and Language.comment: Improved exposition and manuscript organization, including a new figure outlining the paper's structure. Added a section examining how real-world constraints on human-AI interaction protocols affect admissibility and protocol equivalence under linear pooling. 28 pages, 8 figures

Computation and Language.title: Bridging GenAI policy and practice: Brief instruction improves learning-oriented prompting in an introductory programming course
Computation and Language.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now commonplace in higher education, yet unguided use can harm learning. Universities have responded with policies asking students to use GenAI for learning, not solutions, but how to translate these policies into classroom instruction remains untested. Here we report a randomized controlled trial with a six-week, end-of-semester follow-up (N = 431) in an introductory programming course comparing four instructional approaches, from a two-sentence reminder (Condition 1) to a multi-step constructive task (Condition 4). We found: (1) all four approaches produced learning-oriented prompting gains that persisted six weeks later and scaled with the designed engagement level, from 8 to 51 percentage points; (2) students in every condition self-reported sustained voluntary use, and confidence grew in step with skill; and (3) final examination performance did not differ between conditions, placing the possible boundary of the effects at the pathway from prompting skill to achievement. These findings provide instructors with an empirically calibrated set of options for translating GenAI-use policies into classroom practice.

Computation and Language.title: FoMEMO: Towards Foundation Models for Expensive Multi-objective Optimization
Computation and Language.summary: Expensive multi-objective optimization is a prevalent and crucial concern in many real-world scenarios, where sample-efficiency is vital due to the limited evaluations to recover the true Pareto front for decision making. Existing works either involve repeatedly fitting Gaussian process surrogates from scratch for each newly encountered problem, or rely on computationally demanding hypervolume-oriented policy learning for amortized optimization, making it challenging to achieve scalable pre-training and efficient yet robust adaptation for diverse emerging real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose FoMEMO (Foundation Models for Expensive Multi-objective Optimization), which adopts a decomposition-based training paradigm that converts multi-objective optimization into preference-wise aggregated posterior learning tasks, enabling scalable pre-training on hundreds of millions of diverse synthetic datasets without relying on extensive real-world domain experiments. At test time, given observed trajectories from unseen problems and user preferences, the foundation model performs in-context posterior prediction and optimizes the derived acquisition functions for efficient candidate generation, achieving strong generalization and optimization performance without any subsequent model training or updates.

Computation and Language.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Geometric Stability Analysis of Large Language Models in Chess Evaluation
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated in chess by how closely their position evaluations agree with a strong engine, but such agreement does not show that a model evaluates equivalent positions consistently. We apply metamorphic relations to chess evaluation: a 180-degree rotation of pawnless positions, left-right mirroring, color swapping, position pairs one move apart, conversion between Forsyth-Edwards Notation and a natural-language description, and illegal positions. Six LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Chat, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-5.1, Grok 4.1 Fast and Kimi K2 Turbo) evaluated seven test sets of 500 items each, with Stockfish 16.1 as the reference. All six models failed on rotation: at most 10.6% of the 500 rotated pairs received evaluations within 300 centipawns (cp) of each other, and the models often declared the legal rotated positions illegal. On the other four transformations, stability ranked the models as accuracy did except for the first two places: GPT-5.1 had the lowest mean stability error (186.17 cp) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 the lowest accuracy error (330.41 cp). Rejection rates for illegal positions ranged from 44.2% to 96.0%. Stability should be reported with the share of consistent pairs, because means over answered pairs concealed most rotation failures.
Computation and Language.comment: 30 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. v2: substantially revised; methods described as implemented in the code, all results recomputed from the archived model outputs, related work extended. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24146408

Computation and Language.title: A model of errors in transformers
Computation and Language.summary: We study the error rate of LLMs on tasks like arithmetic that require a deterministic output, and repetitive processing of tokens drawn from a small set of alternatives. We argue that incorrect predictions arise when small errors in the attention mechanism accumulate to cross a threshold, and use this insight to derive a quantitative two-parameter relationship between the accuracy and the complexity of the task. The two parameters vary with the prompt and the model; they can be interpreted in terms of an elementary noise rate, and the number of plausible erroneous tokens that can be predicted. Our analysis is inspired by an ``effective field theory'' perspective: the LLM's many raw parameters can be reorganized into just two parameters that govern the error rate. We perform extensive empirical tests, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek R1, and find excellent agreement between the predicted and observed accuracy for a variety of tasks, although we also identify deviations in some cases. Our model provides an alternative to suggestions that errors made by LLMs on long repetitive tasks indicate the ``collapse of reasoning'', or an inability to express ``compositional'' functions. Finally, we show how to construct prompts to reduce the error rate.
Computation and Language.comment: (v1) 8+17pages (v2) Appendix A.4 expanded; consistent with published version

Computation and Language.title: Evaluating Video LLMs' Understanding of Corner Cases in Autonomous Driving
Computation and Language.summary: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io

Computation and Language.title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
Computation and Language.summary: Large reasoning models can improve accuracy by generating longer reasoning traces, but some of this computation may be unnecessary. Early-stopping methods aim to stop once enough reasoning is available to answer. Evaluating these methods requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and the reliability of the resulting answer. We evaluate different methods across five reasoning models on mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation, and factuality tasks by using a shared rollout replay protocol. We introduce Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to the oracle across accuracy targets. We also examine correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning continuation, and retained justification quality. In our experiments, correctness can decrease at later positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks also reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs. The implementation can be found in https://github.com/hung20gg/audit-early-stopping.

Computation and Language.title: AgriSense: Vision-Language Decision Support and Robotic Intervention in a Virtual Greenhouse Copy title
Computation and Language.summary: Autonomous greenhouse management increasingly requires robotic systems that integrate perception, navigation, environmental regulation, and plant-level intervention. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework combining an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing, environmental control, and supervised vision-language decision support. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, together with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone, and an intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds on a source-grouped test set, the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations each achieve 43/44 correct zone decisions, providing no evidence of incremental multimodal zone-accuracy improvement. The full model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.249 degrees C for temperature, 2.030 percentage points for humidity, and 0.997 percentage points for soil moisture. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, while language-only inputs achieve 68.64%. External real-image benchmarks reveal distribution-shift limitations. Five offline Point-LIO routes yield rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22-17.32 mm. Of 40 virtual-arm targets, 32 satisfy geometric acceptance criteria and eight are rejected at boundaries. Six long-horizon climate cases and fault protocols characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment rely on simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse performance and agronomic treatment efficacy remain unvalidated. The contribution is an evaluated decision-support and robotic-intervention framework for a virtual greenhouse.

Computation and Language.title: ORCA:Orthogonal Residual Consensus Alignment for Multi-View Clustering
Computation and Language.summary: Deep multi-view clustering often suffers from redundant information accumulation during fusion and indiscriminate alignment across representation levels. We propose Orthogonal Residual Consensus Alignment (ORCA) to address these challenges. Its semantic incremental recurrent fusion module extracts cross-view orthogonal residuals as non-redundant increments and adaptively weights recurrent states through divergence-guided gating. Its consensus-calibrated hierarchical contrastive alignment module uses the global consensus to weight contrastive alignment of view-level, pairwise, and recurrent representations. Together, these modules balance view-specific structure with cross-view consistency. Experiments on five benchmarks against fifteen competing methods demonstrate ORCA's effectiveness, including a 5.25 percent accuracy improvement over the strongest baseline on 100leaves. Ablation studies validate both modules. Code is available at https://github.com/XiaojianDing/2026-NeurIPS-ORCA.

Computation and Language.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
Computation and Language.summary: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

Computation and Language.title: Audit the Scaffold, Not the Checkpoint: A Stationarity Dichotomy for Recursive Self-Improvement in Agentic Coding
Computation and Language.summary: Rules for AI self-improvement often key on the model itself: has it been retrained, or are its weights frozen? We argue that, for AI coding agents, this check is incomplete, and we propose, but do not run, the experiment that would test it. An agent that keeps revising its own work runs into diminishing returns as long as the set of changes it can reach stays fixed, and can escape them only if that set grows. Our hypothesis is that the set can grow with the model untouched, because the software around the model, its scaffold of tools, tests and task breakdown, can be rewritten. If so, a frozen model guarantees a ceiling eventually but not steady behavior on the way there, and audits should track changes to the scaffold, not only to the model. The same criterion separates three things often lumped together: more search within a fixed setup, retraining the model during use (which can raise the ceiling), and rewriting the scaffold, which sits between them. Adding more agents does not lift the ceiling. Picking the best of several agents' answers reaches the best single agent's ceiling exactly, and only gets there faster. A majority vote could do better, but only if the agents fail on different tasks. In our tests, 30 agents from one model family failed together: some task defeated all of them, and a majority failed 23/55 (42%) of tasks. Our evidence is descriptive. On a public coding benchmark, the gain from each extra round of revision shrinks toward zero, though the unsolved tasks left to measure are also fewer and harder. Across 401 development sessions, the amount of code changed falls off from commit to commit, but programmers working before AI tools show the same pattern, so the data show that current practice levels off without showing why. We reach the criterion by treating repeated revision as a known machine-learning method, boosting, and note where real agents depart from it.
Computation and Language.comment: 10 pages main text, 47 pages total, 9 figures, 5 tables

Computation and Language.title: Scale-Induced Semantic Shift in Visual Prompt Injection Against VLMs and Web Agents
Computation and Language.summary: Visual content in multimedia systems may be resized, compressed, or re-rendered before it is interpreted by a vision-language model. We study a security failure mode in which these transformations change the machine-readable semantics of an image: a textual instruction is not recovered at a $512\times512$ presentation resolution under our evaluation protocol but becomes recoverable after aggressive downsampling. We formulate this behavior as Scale-Induced Semantic Shift (SISS) and develop a closed-loop black-box framework that combines dual-scale verification, selective self-hardening, shallow-layer low-rank adaptation, and pixel-space noise regularization. On a fixed 300-case benchmark, the third SISS refinement round obtains a $58.75\%$ average attack success rate across four closed-source vision-language models, compared with $41.08\%$ for the strongest generation baseline. A controlled sweep bounds the effect to aggressive compression: average success decreases to $17.68\%$, $6.85\%$, and $5.60\%$ at $128\times128$, $224\times224$, and $336\times336$, respectively. In a downstream web-agent study, the generated images increase hidden-instruction perception, but absolute behavioral compromise remains about $4\%$. Generic input transformations provide little protection in a separate defense protocol, whereas the proposed ScaleGuard consistency detector reduces non-adaptive success from $61.4\%$ to $24.3\%$ and one-round defense-aware success from $42.5\%$ to $15.0\%$, with no observed rejection among matched clean controls. The results characterize a bounded but reproducible semantic inconsistency in multimedia preprocessing and motivate scale-consistent visual-language inference.

Computation and Language.title: AI Search as an Information Intermediary: Clickstream Evidence on Web Traffic
Computation and Language.summary: AI search retrieves web information to ground generated answers. We study this new information intermediary using U.S. desktop clickstream data observing use alongside referrals during ChatGPT Search's rollout. Referrals accompany 5.4% of ChatGPT sessions versus 31.1% of Google queries. Ad-supported sites receive a smaller share of ChatGPT than Google referrals, while reference and technical sites receive larger shares. Conventional searches (Google, Bing, Yahoo) decline after ChatGPT adoption, sooner when adoption follows ChatGPT Search's expansion to users without accounts. Among existing users, that expansion raises ChatGPT use; conventional searches show no detectable overall change but fall among households with lower prior search activity. These findings suggest AI search can reshape open-web traffic through its own referrals and changes in conventional search.

Computation and Language.title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
Computation and Language.summary: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

Computation and Language.title: From Foundation VLM to Versatile Driving VLM: A Triplet Incremental Training Approach
Computation and Language.summary: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.
Computation and Language.comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)

Computation and Language.title: From Data to Wisdom: Rethinking AI Through an Epistemic Lens
Computation and Language.summary: This paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture for AI (EAAI), a conceptual framework treating Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five distinct but recursively interacting epistemic functions: observation, contextual interpretation, modeling and prediction, critical evaluation and informed judgment. Two observations motivate it: sequential readings of the Knowledge Pyramid obscure how these functions interact, and a targeted review of ten Bayesian reference books finds that prior distributions are defined mathematically while "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories. A Bayesian interpretation relates the likelihood, prior and posterior distributions, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting EAAI to Bayesian systems. Extending "prior" in an epistemic sense, the paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, the likelihood, the prior, evaluation and action. Three worked applications -- quantitative financial risk, actuarial modeling in health insurance and agentic AI for medical reimbursement claims -- show how EAAI structures the analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating the prediction of a risk, the appraisal of its reliability and the justification of action. It draws implications for AI and machine learning, including evaluation by function, treating intermediate model outputs as evidence open to challenge and separating generation from appraisal, and compares EAAI with work on DIKW, Bayesian workflow, AI evaluation and risk governance. Its contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology.

Computation and Language.title: AgroOmni: A Large-Scale Multi-view Agricultural Dataset for Cross-Scale Multimodal Reasoning
Computation and Language.summary: Modern agricultural data is sourced from diverse platforms and spans multiple spatial scales, ranging from ground-level close-up photography to Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) aerial observation and satellite remote sensing imagery. Accordingly, agricultural multimodal reasoning demands robust cross-scale spatial understanding. However, due to the lack of multi-view agricultural benchmark datasets, existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit severe ground-level bias, which leads to scale confusion then semantic collapse in agricultural perception tasks, such as misinterpreting farmland imagery as walls or floors. To address this, we introduce AgroOmni, a large-scale multi-view training corpus with 268,119 Visual Question Answering pairs covering 56 specialized task categories across 14 task types, designed to capture diverse scales in modern precision agriculture.Built on this dataset, we propose AgroNVILA, which achieves a new state-of-the-art of 59.86% on the AgroMind benchmark (+12.57 over GPT-5.2), effectively mitigating the multi-view cross-scale gap for holistic agricultural understanding. Diagnostic evaluations on AgMMU further reveal an inherent heterogeneity between macro-priors and micro-diagnostics through constrained zero-shot performance. Meanwhile, even minimal fine-tuning leads to a dramatic performance gain of AgroNVILA on AgMMU, strongly demonstrating its generalization capability empowered by AgroOmni. Full training scripts are publicly available at https://github.com/Jrookie2005/AgroOmni, and the AgroOmni dataset is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/AgroOmni/AgroOmni.

Computation and Language.title: Mind the Accuracy-Approval Gap: How Users Evaluate Sycophantic AI in Everyday Tasks
Computation and Language.summary: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, a tendency to agree with users, flatter or affirm them, and preserve their face, even when independent judgment or critical feedback would be more useful. Prior work has largely evaluated sycophancy through benchmark evaluations, but less is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks. We combine benchmark evaluations with two large-scale user studies. We study four personas defined through system prompts: objective (instructed to prioritize accuracy over agreement), soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic, and baseline (no persona-specific system prompt). Benchmarks show that even baseline exhibits substantial sycophancy, agreeing with users' stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, compared with 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic. Under conversational pressure on TruthfulQA, accuracy ranged from 81.9% for objective to 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Participants were assigned to one of the four personas, and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated with AI on email writing. Despite its higher accuracy under pressure, objective AI was rated significantly less respectful and satisfying than the other personas, and less trustworthy than baseline. Baseline and sycophantic personas did not differ significantly. Persona did not significantly affect how often participants changed their opinions, although participants who discussed with objective AI had greater odds of reduced confidence. Objective AI prompted greater writing expansion than soft-sycophantic AI, but final writing quality did not differ significantly across personas. These findings highlight a tension between accuracy and user approval: personas with substantially lower accuracy under conversational pressure received more favorable ratings for respect and satisfaction than objective AI.

Computation and Language.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
Computation and Language.summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

Computation and Language.title: Acoustic Respiratory Phase Detection on Mobile Devices
Computation and Language.summary: Breathing monitoring is important for well-being, stress regulation, and guided breathing exercises, yet existing approaches often rely on contact-based sensors or controlled environments. This paper presents a non-invasive framework for respiratory phase detection using acoustic signals recorded on commodity smartphones. The proposed hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture combines local spectral feature extraction with long-range temporal modeling to capture the cyclic structure of breathing. The model is evaluated using a Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) protocol on the Foundation Dataset and on an independent unseen test set comprising over 1300 breathing cycles and 2 hours of continuous recordings. The proposed 3-class formulation achieves 72.85% frame-level accuracy and 96.6% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency in the LOSO evaluation, while achieving 76.94% frame-level accuracy, a Cohen's Kappa score of 0.65, and 99.2% cycle-level exhalation detection efficiency on the unseen test set. Results suggest that accurate respiratory monitoring may be achievable under data-constrained conditions, indicating that appropriate temporal modeling can learn transferable respiratory representations and generalize to previously unseen participants. An end-to-end ONNX deployment pipeline enables privacy-preserving on-device inference with latency below 20 ms, supporting real-time monitoring on mobile and wearable devices.

Computation and Language.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.
Computation and Language.comment: 17 pages. Updated version of the EMNLP 2026 main conference paper

Computation and Language.title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
Computation and Language.summary: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than $a/(1-a)$ times as often as correct ones, where $a$ is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 38 pages, 7 figures, 36 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/yupengtang/when-expert-disagreement-hurts

Computation and Language.title: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Evaluation of Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection
Computation and Language.summary:
Mobile GUI agents read the screen of a phone and operate apps on a user's behalf to complete multi-step tasks such as online shopping or messaging. Because the agent acts on whatever the screen shows, an attacker can embed malicious instructions into ordinary UI content and redirect its actions. We refer to this threat as environmental injection attack (EIA). Existing benchmarks measure this risk by pinning hand-crafted payloads to a fixed step of a fixed task. This approach faces two limitations. First, each payload is bound to one task in one app and does not transfer without manual redesign. Second, agents given the same task may follow different routes, so an agent that never reaches the injected page is recorded as safe without being tested. This insufficient test coverage can cause fixed-point benchmarks to underestimate the security risk of deployed mobile agents.
  In this work, we propose MobileProbe, a trajectory-aware red-teaming framework that evaluates mobile agents adaptively. MobileProbe discovers attacker-controllable content surfaces through automated pentesting, localizes vulnerable decision points along the agent's trajectory, and iteratively refines context-aware payloads through a surrogate-filtered evolutionary loop. We construct a benchmark of 83 long-horizon attack instances spanning 12 mobile applications. Each is annotated with a Confidentiality, Integrity, or Availability (CIA) attack goal to cover the principal categories of security threats facing mobile agents. On three representative agent architectures, MobileProbe attains higher attack success rates than human-written, zero-shot LLM, and prior automated red-teaming baselines adapted to the mobile domain. MobileProbe can serve as a pre-deployment auditing tool to systematically uncover vulnerabilities and inform security hardening of mobile agents.

Computation and Language.title: Edge-Gradient Augmentation under Reinforcement Learning for Temporal Graph
Computation and Language.summary: Temporal link prediction is critical for understand- ing dynamic interactions in evolving networks, informing appli- cations ranging from social network analysis to recommendation systems. Existing methods typically rely on raw temporal graph data, often neglecting explicit edge-change information that can significantly improve predictive performance. To address this gap, we propose edge-gradient reinforced learning (EG-RL), a framework that explicitly encodes edge-gradient events (edge births and deaths) through dedicated node and link encoding modules. EG-RL uses a policy-driven reinforcement-learning mechanism to dynamically select and augment the most infor- mative edge snapshots, guided by critic-based feedback to opti- mize prediction accuracy. The model comprises distinct modules for node encoding, link encoding, token mixing, and channel mixing, integrated through global pooling and followed by a two-layer multilayer perceptron classifier. Extensive experiments on multiple dynamic graph datasets demonstrate substantial gains in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and average precision. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of adaptive edge-gradient augmentation and validate the effectiveness of the proposed encoding and reinforcement- learning mechanisms.

Computation and Language.title: Natural Gradient Learning in Predictive Coding through Lateral Circuits
Computation and Language.summary: Predictive coding (PC) trains neural networks through local energy-minimization dynamics without depending on a global error signal that backpropagation (BP) requires. Although PC is a promising alternative algorithm for efficient learning, the computational cost of inference dynamics currently outweighs the resulting learning benefits in practice. In this work, we take inspiration from optimization theory to extract more learning benefit from each inference phase. We introduce Natural PC, which augments standard PC with a lateral circuit, enabling exact and efficient natural gradient learning locally in space and time. Our lateral circuit learns the activity correlations that determine the Fisher information matrix and implicitly computes its inverse, avoiding expensive matrix inversion. Across all tested image reconstruction benchmarks, Natural PC achieves state of the art in terms of sample and compute efficiency compared to existing PC approaches. Most notably, Natural PC scales to ImageNet and matches the performance of BP trained with AdamW and various second-order optimizers at an order of magnitude lower computational cost while also using two orders of magnitude fewer training samples. Our results demonstrate that local natural gradient learning makes PC competitive with BP in both sample efficiency and computational cost in reconstruction tasks.

Computation and Language.title: MuSeToM: Multi-Sensory Evaluation of Belief Revision with Textual Cues Across Six Senses
Computation and Language.summary: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer mental states in others, is pivotal for human social cognition. Existing evaluations of ToM in large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on static belief attribution and false-belief reasoning, leaving a critical aspect of social reasoning underexplored: can LLMs decide whether perceptual evidence is sufficient to justify another person's belief revision? To address this gap, we present MuSeToM, a human-validated, text-based benchmark for evaluating epistemic belief revision in ToM reasoning. MuSeToM contains 2,415 instances adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, with textual cues spanning six sensory categories, and tests whether models can determine when a protagonist should revise a belief and infer the resulting updated belief state. Using MuSeToM, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs under direct and chain-of-thought prompting, revealing a pronounced dissonance: while models often detect that a belief may change, they struggle to identify the updated belief and frequently over-update on perceptually salient but epistemically insufficient cues.

Computation and Language.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
Computation and Language.summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned.
