The same allocation structure extends beyond scalar means to vector-valued decision models, including regression and choice/conjoint estimation, by replacing the scalar residual variance with a scalarized sandwich covariance. The value of AI depends not only on model accuracy but also on the operational policy that targets human oversight where it matters most.

Machine Learning.title: Where Has the Foreign Signal Gone? Contributor Composition and the Reliability of Social Media Sentiment
Machine Learning.summary: Social media sentiment is increasingly used to predict stock returns. Its reliability depends on the composition of the crowd generating the feed. For foreign firms, the home-market investors who know them best are underrepresented on English-language Twitter. Hence, their feed should carry a less precise signal. Reduced-form analysis of firm-level Twitter sentiment shows that sentiment noise predicts next-quarter losses less consistently for foreign stocks than for domestic stocks. The loss-on-noise slope is negative in 78 percent of quarters for domestic stocks but in only 48 percent for foreign stocks, with a significant mean difference in slopes. We interpret this difference through a noisy rational expectations model in which the feed carries a public signal produced by three types of contributors. Specialists post repeatedly with information about the firm, attention-driven contributors post once with information about the firm and a transient fad, and automated accounts post repeatedly with no information about the firm. The share of each contributor type and the size of the fad determine the precision of the signal, which, in turn, determines how much of the feed's noise reaches prices. The model gives repeat-author share, fad and precision from the vendor's aggregate metrics, without account-level data, whereas prior work backs out precision from price informativeness. The structural estimates show that feeds for foreign stocks have a higher share of repeat authors, a larger fad component and a less precise signal. Thus, the foreign signal did not disappear but got diluted.

Machine Learning.title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
Machine Learning.summary: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.
Machine Learning.comment: 12 pages, 2 figures with the IEEE Transactions template

Machine Learning.title: Do we really need the Rademacher complexities?
Machine Learning.summary:
We study the fundamental problem of learning with respect to the squared loss in a convex class. In the subgaussian setting, the sharpest known sample complexity bounds are characterised via fixed points associated with the limiting gaussian process. In more general settings (for example, heavier-tailed scenarios) the state-of-the-art bounds rely on localised Rademacher complexities, which are often difficult to control and can be considerably larger than their limiting gaussian counterparts.
  We show that if one has access to coarse information on the covariance structure of the underlying class, it is possible to derive an upper bound on the sample complexity that matches the state-of-the-art rates in the gaussian setting---even in heavy-tailed regimes. As a consequence, under rather minimal assumptions, learning problems that share the same $L_2$-structure---even those involving heavy-tailed distributions---admit the same upper bound on the sample complexity as if the problem were fully gaussian. This constitutes the first universality result for general convex learning problems.
  The proof is based on a novel learning procedure, and its performance is studied by combining optimal mean estimation techniques for real-valued random variables with Talagrand's generic chaining method.

Machine Learning.title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
Machine Learning.summary: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.

Machine Learning.title: Minimax Rates and Spectral Distillation for Tree Ensembles
Machine Learning.summary: Tree ensembles such as random forests (RFs) and gradient boosting machines (GBMs) are among the most widely used supervised learners, yet their theoretical properties remain incompletely understood. We adopt a spectral perspective on these algorithms, with two main contributions. First, we derive minimax-optimal convergence for RF regression, showing that, under mild regularity conditions on tree growth, the eigenvalue decay of the induced kernel operator governs the statistical rate. Second, we exploit this spectral viewpoint to develop compression schemes for tree ensembles. For RFs, leading eigenfunctions of the kernel operator capture the dominant predictive directions; for GBMs, leading singular vectors of the smoother matrix play an analogous role. Learning nonlinear maps for these spectral representations yields distilled models that are orders of magnitude smaller than the originals while maintaining competitive predictive performance. Our methods compare favorably to state of the art algorithms for forest pruning and rule extraction, with applications to resource constrained computing.
Machine Learning.comment: NeurIPS camera ready version. 10 pages main text, 48 pages total (excluding checklist), with 12 figures and 10 tables total

Machine Learning.title: Outliers and the Hard-Margin Linear SVM in High-Dimension, Low-Sample-Size Settings
Machine Learning.summary: We study how outliers affect the hard-margin linear support vector machine when the dimension grows while the sample sizes remain fixed. For one-sided contamination, the centered Gram matrix converges to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, and the limiting dual problem has a closed-form solution. All outliers act through one effective distance. This representation yields explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage. intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. We then treat contamination in both classes. The limiting intercept is the multiplier of the class-balance constraint, and the two classes pull it in opposite directions. Consequently, at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, whereas symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks. Seven numerical experiments verify the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.

Machine Learning.title: Eigenvalues of the Hessian in Deep Learning: The Origin of Symmetry and Its Breaking
Machine Learning.summary:
Hessian spectra at trained models in deep learning exhibit a persistent pattern: eigenvalues organize into distinct clusters, including a large bulk near zero and a few isolated outliers. This paper shows that a natural account of these spectral phenomena emerges when the original setting is understood as a departure from a nearby, otherwise hidden, highly symmetric reference.
  Modifications, including changes to the architecture, data distribution, or parameter metric, expose a nearby reference configuration whose Hessian exhibits rich invariances-ones not accounted for by weight symmetries. There, symmetry enables a precise description of the spectra, forcing high-dimensional kernels and eigenvalues of large multiplicity. Returning to the original configuration breaks the Hessian symmetry and thereby produces the observed hierarchy of clusters and outliers.
  The framework is developed in some generality, with a detailed analysis of three-layer ReLU networks and applications to convolutional, graph, and transformer models, as well as to the NTK. The same mechanism is further shown to yield analogous spectral structures in layerwise Hessians and the Gauss-Newton matrix.

Machine Learning.title: Beyond Interaction Scores: Selecting Feature Interactions via Independent Replication
Machine Learning.summary: Learning feature interactions is essential for accurate prediction and interpretable modeling, yet a high interaction score may reflect fitting noise rather than a reproducible pattern. Ranking methods score feature pairs but leave the cutoff to the user; testing methods set the cutoff but rely on repeated model refits or a model of the joint feature distribution. We present LENS, a model-agnostic framework for selecting feature interactions through independent replication. LENS trains two models with the same learning algorithm on disjoint data and accesses them only through predictions. For each feature pair, it removes main effects from the joint-effect surface to isolate an interaction pattern, ranks pairs by its strength, and tests whether the second model reproduces it at a meaningful strength. A single multiple-testing correction determines which pairs to retain, using only two model fits regardless of the number of features. We prove that a replication ratio alone can retain arbitrarily weak patterns shared by both fits, whereas a strength floor restores selection consistency, and we characterize when normalization in Friedman's $H^2$ reverses interaction rankings. On 16 synthetic designs, LENS matches leading model-specific ranking methods (e.g., TreeSHAP) and recovers 91% of material interactions, against 45% for the knockoff-based DIAMOND, without selecting false pairs; with 1,225 candidate pairs and no interactions, it makes substantially fewer false discoveries. On large-scale French motor insurance data, it identifies interactions documented in the actuarial literature and recovers 90% of the deviance gain obtained using all pairs. On two credit datasets, LENS selects few pairs while maintaining or slightly improving predictive performance over the additive baseline.

Machine Learning.title: Factor Augmented High-Dimensional SGD
Machine Learning.summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a fundamental optimization algorithm widely used in modern machine learning. In this paper, we propose Factor-Augmented SGD (FSGD), a new optimization method that leverages latent factor representations in high-dimensional learning tasks. Unlike standard two-stage dimension reduction approaches that rely on offline representation learning and full data storage, a key novelty of FSGD is that it operates purely on streaming data, making it scalable to large-scale and high-dimensional problems. Furthermore, we establish the first theoretical framework that explicitly incorporates latent factor estimation error into the analysis of SGD, and provide moment convergence in $\ell^s$ norm under decaying step sizes and mini-batch updates. Our results provide a new foundation for employing SGD reliably and scalably in high-dimensional machine learning systems.

Machine Learning.title: A Distribution Mapping Approach to Counterfactually Fair Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to optimize sequential decisions to maximize population-level benefits over time. However, when deployed in high-stakes settings such as healthcare, RL decisions might systematically restrict some subpopulation's access to valuable services in a manner contrary to the values and goals of stakeholders. Counterfactual fairness (CF) offers a promising framework to address this problem based on causal reasoning. This paper develops a data preprocessing algorithm that, when used in tandem with policy learning, enables CF in RL. Our algorithm relies on a novel quantile distribution mapping method for sequentially estimating the counterfactual states and rewards in the data preprocessing step, subsuming common additivity assumptions used for counterfactual prediction as a special case. We theoretically prove that the per-step level of counterfactual unfairness and infinite-horizon suboptimality gap can be bounded under mild regularity conditions. We also empirically test our algorithm in numerical experiments as well as in application to a real-world interventional digital health dataset.

Machine Learning.title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
Machine Learning.summary: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = ρ/ (μ_i + ρ)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $Δ_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $Ψ(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $ω^* = (4ν^2 Σ/ c')^{1/3}$, $c' = σ^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(ρ)$, and the plug-in strength $ρ^* = σ^2 / (nδ^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $ρ_{\mathrm{eff}} = ρ(e^{ζq} - 1) / (ζq)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.
Machine Learning.comment: 67 pages, 7 figures. Lean 4 formalization and code: [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23768172](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23768172)

Machine Learning.title: CP-MLPs: A Tensor-Rank Theory of Tied and Untied MLP Blocks
Machine Learning.summary: Transformer feed-forward blocks combine several design choices: squared activations, gating, and tied versus untied parameter sharing, whose separate contributions to expressivity remain poorly understood. We introduce CP-MLPs, a tensor framework in which each multiplicative unit contributes a rank-1 interaction with three roles: detecting an input feature, reading a value, and writing to the output. Tied gated blocks such as ReLU$^2$ force the detector and value roles to share the same direction; untied gated blocks such as ReGLU and SwiGLU let them differ. We show that this distinction yields exact, degree-wise tensor-rank separations: untied detector-value units are strictly more width-efficient for indefinite quadratic interactions and role-asymmetric monomials, while tied units are structurally matched to symmetric pure-power targets. The width advantage of untying therefore depends on the target structure. Experiments show loss plateaus below the exact-representation width, but these plateaus alone do not establish a positive approximation gap: arbitrarily accurate approximation is governed by border rank. In trained gated MLPs, untied blocks retain an advantage in selected comparisons at matched input-projection budget. Code is available at https://github.com/rarefin/CP-MLPs.

Machine Learning.title: First-order asymptotic expansions for spectral convergence of normalized graph Laplacians constructed from samples on manifolds
Machine Learning.summary: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed Riemannian manifold embedded in Euclidean space, we derive first-order asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians constructed via Gaussian kernels and provide concentration inequalities for the remainder terms. As a direct consequence, we establish the corresponding weak convergence results. Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.

Machine Learning.title: Investigating Composite Modeling in Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Design
Machine Learning.summary: Scientific design often requires balancing competing objectives that are expensive to evaluate through experiments or simulations. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) addresses this challenge by using probabilistic models to guide the selection of promising designs. In many applications, tunable inputs map to observable intermediate responses, which are then combined through known functions to compute the final objectives. Prior work on Bayesian optimization of composite functions shows that learning from these intermediate responses, which we call Composite modeling, can substantially improve sampling efficiency in single-objective optimization, compared to methods that condition only on black-box observations of the objective function. The benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO, however, remain understudied. In this work, we study the benefits of Composite modeling in MOBO and investigate the factors driving variation in its gains. We first establish single-objective conditions under which intermediate observations provide no additional predictive information beyond objective values, where composite and black box methods use the same warped Gaussian process prior. Controlled numerical experiments with versions of four MOBO methods across eight synthetic and application-inspired scientific-design benchmarks examine how these conditions relate to optimization gains in the multi-objective setting, where the black box approach models the objective functions with a standard multi-output Gaussian process. Both investigations support the claim that composite modeling tends to help more when the function mapping intermediate responses to final objectives is non-bijective and non-affine.

Machine Learning.title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
Machine Learning.summary: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.

Machine Learning.title: Simultaneous Near-Optimal Region Identification in Continuous Simulation Optimization: Minimax Complexity and Adaptive Sampling
Machine Learning.summary: Simulation optimization typically returns a single estimated optimal point. When decisions also depend on criteria evaluated independently of simulation, such as resource cost, the decision maker instead needs the set of designs whose expected performance lies within a tolerance of the optimum, often choosing the tolerance only after seeing the tradeoffs. We study how to identify these near-optimal regions on a continuous design space, simultaneously for all tolerances up to a prescribed maximum $T$, with region estimation error at most $η$. We show that region identification is not a by-product of optimization. Specifically, when $α>ν$, any procedure, even one given the optimal design in advance, needs at least $Ω\bigl(η^{-(2+d/ν)}\min\{1,KT^{d/α}\}\bigr)$ simulation evaluations, where $d$ is the dimension, $ν$ the smoothness, and $(K,α)$ the covering parameters that describe the geometry of the near-optimal designs. We propose SASORI, which returns an estimated optimal point and the regions for all tolerances from the same evaluations, matching this lower bound up to logarithmic factors. SASORI also achieves the optimal tradeoff between region estimation error and cumulative regret, and reduces to a minimax-optimal simulation optimization procedure at zero tolerance. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

Machine Learning.title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
Machine Learning.summary: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.

Machine Learning.title: Posterior Contraction Rates for Sparse Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Anisotropic Besov Spaces
Machine Learning.summary: We study posterior contraction rates for sparse Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) over anisotropic Besov spaces, providing a statistical foundation for KANs from a Bayesian point of view. We show that sparse Bayesian KANs equipped with spike-and-slab-type sparsity priors attain a near-minimax posterior contraction rate. In particular, the contraction rate depends on the intrinsic anisotropic smoothness of the underlying function. Moreover, by placing a hyperprior on a single model-size parameter, the resulting posterior adapts to unknown anisotropic smoothness and still achieves the corresponding near-minimax rate. A distinctive feature of our results, compared with those for standard multilayer perceptrons, is that the KAN depth can be kept fixed: owing to the expressive power of learnable spline edge functions, the required approximation complexity is controlled through the network width, the range and size of the spline grid, and parameter sparsity. Our analysis develops theoretical tools tailored to sparse spline-edge architectures, including approximation and complexity bounds for Bayesian KANs. We then extend to compositional Besov spaces and show that the contraction rates depend on layerwise smoothness and effective dimension of the underlying compositional structure, thereby effectively avoiding the curse of dimensionality. Together, these results advance the theoretical understanding of Bayesian neural networks and establish rigorous Bayesian guarantees for KANs.

Machine Learning.title: Sufficient Dimension Reduction with Multimodal Predictor Objects
Machine Learning.summary: We study the regression of a scalar response $Y$ on a Euclidean predictor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ and a random predictor object $\mathcal{Z}$ in a general metric space under arbitrary structural dependence. We introduce a joint sufficient dimension reduction $(\mathbf{B}^\top\mathbf{X}, \mathcal{G}_Z)$ constructed via a sequential conditional independence framework, which differs fundamentally from the ordinary central subspace of $Y \mid \mathbf{X}$. Methodologically, $\mathcal{Z}$ is embedded into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and a regularized kernel-response envelope model extracts a finite-dimensional reduction of the feature map. Partial adaptive estimation then recovers the Euclidean reduction conditional on the first-stage coordinates. We establish root-$n$ consistency rates for the first-stage envelope subspace under a shrinking regularizer, alongside large-sample consistency for the second-stage Euclidean subspace estimator. Simulations and two real-data applications illustrate the utility and flexibility of the proposed method.

Machine Learning.title: The Star Geometry of Critic-Based Regularizer Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Variational regularization is a classical technique to solve statistical inference tasks and inverse problems, with modern data-driven approaches parameterizing regularizers via deep neural networks showcasing impressive empirical performance. Recent works along these lines learn task-dependent regularizers. This is done by integrating information about the measurements and ground-truth data in an unsupervised, critic-based loss function, where the regularizer attributes low values to likely data and high values to unlikely data. However, there is little theory about the structure of regularizers learned via this process and how it relates to the two data distributions. To make progress on this challenge, we initiate a study of optimizing critic-based loss functions to learn regularizers over a particular family of regularizers: gauges (or Minkowski functionals) of star-shaped bodies. This family contains regularizers that are commonly employed in practice and shares properties with regularizers parameterized by deep neural networks. We specifically investigate critic-based losses derived from variational representations of statistical distances between probability measures. By leveraging tools from star geometry and dual Brunn-Minkowski theory, we illustrate how these losses can be interpreted as dual mixed volumes that depend on the data distribution. This allows us to derive exact expressions for the optimal regularizer in certain cases. Finally, we identify which neural network architectures give rise to such star body gauges and when do such regularizers have favorable properties for optimization. More broadly, this work highlights how the tools of star geometry can aid in understanding the geometry of unsupervised regularizer learning.

Machine Learning.title: Settling the Burn-in Gap: Sharp Risk Bounds for Tail-Averaged SGD in Linear Regression
Machine Learning.summary: We study the excess risk of constant-stepsize online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with tail-averaging for high-dimensional linear regression. Building on the instance-dependent spectral framework of Zou et al. (2021), we establish matching initialization-explicit upper and lower bounds on the total excess risk of tail-averaged SGD in terms of the population covariance spectrum $\mathbf{H}$ and initialization $\mathbf{w}_0-\mathbf{w}^*$ whenever a trajectory spectral feedback condition holds. Existing analyses exhibit a fundamental gap in the effective variance: the upper bound of Zou et al. (2021) retains an undamped contribution from the initial error in the head eigenspace $\mathbf{I}_{0:k^\dagger}$, whereas their lower bound omits the variance induced by the head initialization altogether. We show that both the existing upper and lower bounds are loose: the single-hop fast-mode variance contribution from the head initialization is exponentially damped during the burn-in phase, whereas fourth-moment energy scattered from the head initialization into slow spectral modes during the early burn-in steps survives undamped into the averaging window. We prove that our spectral feedback condition is satisfied in two concrete constant-stepsize regimes: (i) for arbitrary covariance spectra $\mathbf{H}$ and any finite horizon, under an explicit horizon-dependent stepsize chosen prior to execution; and (ii) for polynomially decaying spectra $λ_i\asymp i^{-a}$ ($a>1$), under a single horizon-independent positive stepsize. Finally, we complement these positive results with explicit one- and two-dimensional separation constructions proving an exponential-versus-polynomial gap in the lower bound of Zou et al. (2021) and showing why fourth-moment assumptions alone cannot determine the asymptotic exponential decay rate without additional structural conditions.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Enforcing Axioms for AI Alignment under Loss-Based Rules
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Many alignment methods, most notably reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), train reward models by minimizing a loss on pairwise comparisons of model responses. Inspired by principle-guided methods such as Constitutional AI, we treat each principle as a voter that compares responses according to that principle, for example, preferring the more helpful or less toxic response. We represent these voters as linear directions in a fixed embedding space, a simplifying assumption motivated by the Linear Representation Hypothesis. In this linear social choice model, Ge et al. (2024) showed that an optimal linear reward model can violate Pareto optimality (PO): From the principles-as-voters lens, this means a response A can be less helpful and more toxic than B, yet still receive a higher reward. We ask whether richer reward models or changes to comparison data can recover PO within loss-based training. We show that PO can still fail for polynomials of any fixed degree and one-hidden-layer ReLU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) of any fixed width $ d\ge 2 $ with suitable finite parameter bounds. We then recover PO for loss-based training of linear rewards under suitable assumptions in an idealized setting with uniform comparison directions and equal comparison lengths. These results motivate dataset design as an approach to recovering PO in constitutional-style alignment while retaining loss-based training.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICLR 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Choosing Complexity: Cognitive Ability, Overconfidence, and Task Choice
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Workers and organizations routinely choose between complex tasks that differ in their success-payment tradeoff. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. In about 75% of the decisions, subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability is weakly associated with more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly one-sided: those who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 71 pages, including appendices. JEL: C91, D03, D83, D91, J24

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Splitting for Stability: a Modified Reward Scheme for Transaction-Fee-Only Regimes
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
As Bitcoin's block subsidy declines over time, miner revenue will come to depend increasingly on transaction fees. In fee-dominated regimes, winner-take-all reward structures can create incentives for undercutting and fork-based mining strategies, leading to instability and reduced transaction throughput.
  To prevent this instability, we propose a reward-splitting mechanism in which the winning block producer receives an $α$-portion of the block reward, while the rest is distributed among other miners; this incentivizes mining on previous blocks with higher rewards, while preserving the incentive to produce blocks with high rewards.
  We evaluate the proposed reward structure through analysis and simulation. Our analysis derives a local profitability condition for one-step Function-Fork deviations, showing how the winner-side reward, loser-side subsidy, and honest hash power jointly determine whether undercutting is profitable. Simulations show parameter regions in which honest behavior dominates fork-based deviations. In the cases where forking becomes dominant, the learned strategy is the least aggressive variant studied. The analysis and simulations suggest that suitable reward-splitting parameters can reduce the honest participation needed to suppress aggressive forking strategies relative to the winner-take-all structure studied in prior work. Finally, we show that the modified reward scheme does not appear to worsen selfish mining incentives.
  Together, these results suggest that reward redistribution can mitigate fee-driven fork incentives without introducing stronger selfish mining incentives, providing a possible direction for incentive design in fee-era proof-of-work systems.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic investment and coordination in teams: Theory and experimental evidence
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Teamwork requires more than the general skills that team members bring. In successful teams, members invest in team-specific skill or capital that accumulates within the team and raises the return to coordinated production. We provide the first systematic analysis of dynamic investment in such team skill. Adopting a dynamic game approach, we develop a novel theoretical framework where investment in team skill creates persistent benefits but is risky because the benefits depend on successful team coordination. We then take this framework to the laboratory to study empirically the factors that influence dynamic investment in team skill. We find underinvestment compared to the efficient benchmark. However, investment responds strongly to incentives, in line with specific theory-predicted patterns. Pre-registered traits (theory of mind and propensity to coordinate) predict investment and team-level efficiency. We conclude that careful design of team incentives and selection of team members can facilitate the development of team skill.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 90 pages, including appendices. JEL: C73, C92, D91, J24

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: An Improved $(1+2e)$-Approximation Algorithm for Metric Data Placement
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the metric data placement problem with site-capacity constraints and fixed installation costs, aiming to minimize the total cost of placing data (resources) and accessing their nearest copies. We develop a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm based on a natural linear programming relaxation of the problem. Starting from an optimal fractional solution, we construct multiscale metric-ball partitions independently for each resource and connect overlapping balls at consecutive levels to form a flow network. The resource layers are then coupled through shared site-capacity arcs, allowing us to obtain an integral placement by minimizing a surrogate cost over a single min-cost circulation. By optimizing the choice of ball radii, we establish an approximation factor of $1+2e\approx 6.44$. To our knowledge, this is the best approximation guarantee for the metric data placement problem since its introduction by Baev and Rajaraman in 2001.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Useful Work Can Increase Energy Use: Demand Elasticity and Proof of Useful Work
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
A serious criticism of Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work is its enormous electricity consumption. Proof-of-Useful-Work (PoUW), introduced by Ball, Rosen, Sabin, and Vasudevan (2017), in which mining performs useful computations, was suggested as an alternative to reduce electricity expenditure, with matrix multiplication (MatMul) as a recent concrete instantiation by Komargodski and Weinstein (2026).
  Perhaps surprisingly, we show that switching to PoUW may increase the total electricity consumption, echoing Jevons' paradox. Intuitively, the PoUW mechanism acts as a subsidy that lowers the effective price of the useful work. Recall that demand is elastic if a discount of x percent in the price leads to an increase of more than x percent in the quantity demanded. If demand is elastic, the resulting increase in quantity demanded leads to a net increase in total electricity consumption; if inelastic, total electricity consumption decreases. Even then, the electricity consumption due to PoUW never vanishes, since the mining subsidy is spent on useful work that would not have been produced without the subsidy. This result is proved in a simple model with electricity-only costs, no PoUW overhead, and an unchanged mining subsidy. The analysis extends to less restrictive settings with adjusted thresholds.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 24 pages, 1 figure

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Fractional Pareto-Optimality in Multiwinner Voting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Efficiency in multiwinner voting is most naturally captured by Pareto-optimality (PO), yet this notion is computationally and structurally difficult to handle. We therefore study fractional Pareto-optimality (fPO), under which a committee may not be dominated even by a fractional committee, i.e., any convex combination of committees. fPO turns out to be a natural refinement of PO as it retains exactly those Pareto-optimal committees whose efficiency is robust under uniform cloning of candidates. Furthermore, fPO committees are guaranteed to exist and have strong structural properties. We present a characterization of fPO in terms of weighted utilitarian welfare maximization, which yields a polynomial-time algorithm for verifying fPO and shows that the set of fPO committees satisfies committee monotonicity and is connected under single-candidate swaps. Analyzing welfarist rules through the lens of fPO, we further uncover an incompatibility between fPO and equality-oriented objectives. Most notably, we show that proportional approval voting (PAV) violates fPO in the approval setting. We close by pinpointing preference domains, including various one-dimensional ones, on which PO and fPO collapse into one notion.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning to Choose with Categories: Theory and an Application to Algorithmic Prominence
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We introduce Coarse Q-learning, a reinforcement learning framework in which a decision-maker partitions alternatives into coarse similarity classes, chooses among available classes using logit, and learns class valuations by averaging experienced payoffs. Even in stationary bandit problems with independently drawn menus, choices change the composition of pooled feedback. By deriving the continuous-time mean field ODE limit, we show this endogenous sampling can generate a unique globally attracting mixed equilibrium with limiting indifference, multiple stable strict rankings, or persistent cycling. Learning can reduce welfare even when the coarse representation admits efficient choice. An application demonstrates how digital platforms may exploit this feedback by promoting high-quality products to sustain purchases of inferior products under a common brand.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 45 Main pages + 92 Supplemental Appendix pages

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Elicitation of the parameters of a multi-criteria sorting model
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Multiple-criteria decision aiding (MCDA) proposes models and methods for different types of decision problems such as choice, ranking or sorting. Such models involve various parameters that must be elicited. In the elicitation process, all necessary information has to be taken from the decision-maker. For this, several direct and indirect elicitation methods are suggested in the literature. In this work, we concentrate on direct elicitation: we aim at providing a rigorous elicitation procedure for the parameters of the Non-Compensatory Sorting model (NCS), which has been characterized by an axiomatic analysis. A basic version of the NCS model is considered, i.e., a model with two categories and no vetoes. The parameters are the set of sufficient coalitions of criteria and the profile separating the two categories. Regarding the sufficient coalitions, we propose several questioning algorithms that engraft questions on classical graph exploration algorithms such as depth-first search. Such algorithms are implemented and evaluated by simulation. For eliciting the limit profile, we design a questioning algorithm using dichotomy. Questioning algorithms can be optimal in the worst case or on average. An optimal algorithm in the worst case has been proposed by Hansel in the framework of monotone Boolean functions. We implement and evaluate this algorithm as a variant of the depth-first search approaches. Regarding optimal questioning strategies on average, we evaluate decision trees for up to four criteria. On the other hand, we assess how more general is NCS as compared to MR-Sort, a particular case of the NCS model in which sufficient coalitions can be represented by additive weights.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: PhD Thesis defended at University of Mons, Belgium, July 07 2023. 216 pages https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12907/57144

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Modelling Opinion Dynamics at Scale with Deep MARL
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Modelling opinion dynamics typically relies on hand-crafted local interaction rules to study emergent macroscopic phenomena such as consensus and polarisation. In contrast, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables agents to learn such behaviours directly by optimising simple rewards. To explore the potential of MARL for opinion dynamics, we introduce a GPU-accelerated consensus and truth-finding game that scales to populations of up to 1000 agents, comparable to many real-world social sub-networks. To prevent unrealistic conventions, we extend other-play to general-sum social interactions. We next validate our model on a subset of the Bluesky network by recovering agent importance structures from graph topology alone via a learned attention layer, finding that highly conforming populations most closely match human data. In large social media networks, such high levels of conformity significantly reduce collective accuracy and promote dishonest agents that lie to fit in. By contrast, small hunter-gatherer networks are less affected; here, conformity can even improve collective agreement. This suggests a mismatch between evolved human conformity heuristics and modern social media environments as a potential contributor to misinformation.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 39 pages, 31 figures. Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the fair allocation of indivisible items to agents with budget constraints and additive valuations. Each agent compares its own bundle with the subsets of another bundle that fit its budget. An allocation is envy-free up to one item (EF1) if, for every agent and every nonempty subset under comparison, removing an item of maximum value to that agent eliminates its envy. We require EF1 both between agents and towards the charity, which contains all unallocated items. EF1 allocations exist, but computing them in polynomial time has remained open even for homogeneous valuations. We resolve this problem with a polynomial-time algorithm for EF1 allocations under heterogeneous valuations. We also prove that detecting an EF1 violation is NP-complete. Equivalently, checking whether a given allocation is EF1 is coNP-complete. Finally, we give polynomial-time algorithms for envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) both when each agent's valuation is proportional to item size and when each agent has a fixed number of distinct positive item values. As an application, for homogeneous valuations and any $\varepsilon>0$, we obtain an EF1 allocation with at least a $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ fraction of the maximum social welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Smoothed Analysis of Nash Equilibrium and Fixed Point Computation, and Efficiency of the Homotopy Method
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study, under a smoothed analysis perspective, the complexity of three PPAD-complete problems: computing Nash equilibria, computing fixed points, and solving variational inequalities. We consider a general perturbation model that bounds the probability density of the quantities evaluated by our algorithms. As special cases, it captures worst-case games perturbed by small random per-action costs, and worst-case maps perturbed by a small random affine function.
  Under these models, we show that classical algorithmic paradigms, cover-based search and homotopy path-following provably outperform the worst-case state-of-the-art. For games with a constant number of players and $n$ strategies per player, a recursive cover-based algorithm computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium using $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$ expected payoff-vector computations, compared to the worst-case runtime tradeoffs of $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot n^{O(n)}$, $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$, $2^{O(\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)}$, and $2^{O(n)}\mathrm{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. For fixed points and variational inequalities of bounded and Lipschitz maps on the $n$-dimensional $\ell_2$ unit ball, the same approach runs in expected time $\log(1/\varepsilon)\cdot 2^{O(n)}$, compared to the worst-case $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(n)}$; the $2^{Ω(n)}$ factor is necessary by prior work [Rubinstein, 2017]. For general smooth maps, we further analyze the classical predictor--corrector homotopy method, for which only qualitative convergence guarantees were previously known, showing that under perturbations the homotopy path is well conditioned and has length $2^{O(n)}$, so that the method finds an $\varepsilon$-approximate solution in time $2^{O(n)}\cdot\mathrm{poly}(1/p)/\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-p$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning Global Equilibria in Non-Concave Prospect Theoretic Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Human agents in non cooperative games often exhibit non rational behaviour. Prospect theory provides a behavioural framework to capture how agents perceive gains and losses under risk, but, its incorporation into games typically leads to non concave and non convex utility functions, making equilibrium computation challenging. In such cases, it is difficult to obtain algorithms that have global convergence behaviour. This paper proposes a learning algorithm which uses minorization-maximization (MM). Under a proximal Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition on the potential function, we establish global convergence of the algorithm to a potential-maximizing Nash equilibrium. We further show how the structure of the MM minorizer can be used to enable a distributed implementation of the algorithm. With additional noise injection, the individual updates of the agents can be obscured, while still ensuring global convergence.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning Equilibria in Coordination Games via Minorization-Maximization
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: This paper considers games where the utilities for agents are the sum of a term proportional to a social utility, and another term that is an individual cost or reward. The agents are assumed to be irrational in their perception of the individual cost or reward. The multi equilibrium game is regularized, and its strictly concave potential function is used to select a unique equilibrium. This selected equilibrium is shown to be an $ε-$equilibrium of the original game, where $ε$ is parametrized by the regularizing function. A minorization-maximization based iterative learning scheme is proposed to learn equilibria in this game. This scheme converges to the potential-optimal equilibrium, and has superior convergence behavior in comparison to gradient and best response methods.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Existence of Maximin Share Allocations is $Δ_2^P$-complete
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The maximin share (MMS) guarantee has become one of the central fairness benchmarks for allocating indivisible items. Since Kurokawa, Procaccia, and Wang [EC'14, JACM'18] showed that exact MMS allocations need not exist, a substantial literature has developed around the existence and computation of approximate MMS allocations, including the recent work of Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin, and Shahrezaei [SODA'26]. In contrast, a fundamental complexity question posed more than a decade ago by Bouveret and Lemaître [JAAMAS'16] has remained unresolved: how hard is it to decide whether an exact MMS allocation exists?
  For additive valuations, Lonc and Truszczynski [JAIR'20] established membership in the complexity class $Δ_2^P$ (also known as $P^{NP}$), but no hardness result was known. For the more general class of 2-additive valuations, Bouveret and Lemaître established NP-hardness, leaving a substantial gap to the $Δ_2^P$ upper bound. Moreover, the complexity of MMS existence for additive and $k$-additive valuations was posed as open questions.
  We resolve this longstanding question by proving that deciding the existence of an MMS allocation for additive goods is $Δ_2^P$-complete, even for five agents.
  Additionally, we prove weak coNP-hardness for three agents, thereby establishing a precise dichotomy with the known existence guarantee for two agents, and strong coNP-hardness when the number of agents is unrestricted. Furthermore, our strong hardness construction yields an inverse-polynomial gap in the optimal MMS approximation ratio, ruling out an FPTAS for approximating this ratio unless P=NP. Finally, we show that all these results for goods extend to the chores setting through a polynomial-time transformation that preserves MMS existence.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 58 pages; this version strengthens the main result for additive valuations; abstract shortened to meet arXiv requirements

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: When Everyone Can Submit: Designing Contests with Transparent Pre-Selection
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Shortlisting is a common and effective method for pre-selecting participants in competitive settings. To ensure fairness, a cut-off score is typically announced, allowing only contestants who exceed it to enter the contest, while others are eliminated. In this paper, we study rank-order contests with shortlisting and cut-off score disclosure. We fully characterize the equilibrium behavior of shortlisted contestants for any given prize structure and shortlist size. We examine two objective functions: the highest individual performance and total performance. Under linear performance costs, for both objectives, the optimal contest is in a winner-take-all format. For the highest individual performance, the optimal shortlist size is exactly two contestants, but, in contrast, for total performance, the shortlist size does not affect the outcome, i.e., any size yields the same total performance. Furthermore, we compare the highest individual performance achieved with and without shortlisting, and show that the former is 4/3 of the latter.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: NeurIPS 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Strategy-robust Online Learning in Contextual Pricing
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Learning effective pricing strategies is crucial in digital marketplaces, especially when buyers' valuations are unknown and must be inferred through interaction. We study online contextual pricing with sealed bids from multiple recurring buyers. The seller selects an affine pricing policy before observing the current context and competes with the best fixed policy in the same class. Buyers may misreport their values to influence future prices, a challenge known as strategic overfitting (Amin et. al., 2013).
  We introduce a strategy-robust notion of regret for multi-buyer online environments, capturing worst-case strategic behavior in the spirit of the Price of Anarchy. Our first contribution is a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for learning affine pricing policies against arbitrary context-value sequences: for every fixed $ε>0$, it runs in polynomial time and its regret is $O(εT)$ plus a term sublinear in $T$. The scheme is based on an online sketch constructed from past contexts. We then propose the Sparse Update Mechanism (SUM), which learns only from a privately selected subset of rounds and occasionally posts a random price drawn from a finite grid. SUM is a PTAS for strategic regret, and its guarantee holds uniformly over all Nash equilibria. Both schemes use an online expert algorithm as a black box and run in $(T/ε)^{O(ε^{-2})}\mathsf{poly}(d,T,1/ε)$ time. Furthermore, we show that, even with truthful bids, no seller algorithm can achieve regret $\mathsf{poly}(d,1/ε)\,T^z+εT$ with $z<1$ in time $\mathsf{poly}(d,T,1/ε)$ unless $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}$.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 30 pages. v3 is the preliminary version published at ALT 2026. This version extends the results to affine pricing policies, improves the regret and running-time bounds, and bases the lower bound on NP-hardness rather than ETH, which was recently claimed to be false

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: GAE Falls Short in Imperfect-Information Self-Play Reinforcement Learning
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning in imperfect-information games requires agents to act under partial observability and against adversarial opponents, necessitating stochastic policies. While self-play reinforcement learning with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has achieved strong empirical success, its standard advantage estimator, generalized advantage estimation, suffers from additional variance due to the sampling of stochastic future actions. This variance is amplified in equilibrium self-play because of the stochastic nature of the equilibrium policy and persists even when the critic is exact. We address this bottleneck by introducing $Q$-boosting, a variance-reduced advantage estimator based on a centralized action-value critic, and propose Variance-Reduced Policy Optimization (VRPO), incorporating this new estimator. The algorithm replaces sampled multi-step backups with a multi-step Expected SARSA$(λ)$ trace, computing policy expectations at each step to average out action-sampling noise, while retaining PPO's clipped objective and on-policy actor updates. Empirically, VRPO achieves strong performance in various games: In mid-sized games where exploitability is computable, VRPO lowers the exact exploitability by more than 15% compared to tuned baselines. In Dou Dizhu, it sets a new state of the art over PerfectDou. In Heads-Up No-Limit Texas Hold'em, it posts a positive win rate against Slumbot without any blueprint raise sizes, search, or subgame solving at test time.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Tropical Gaussian Anticoncentration: Optimal Instance-Dependent Bounds for Online Learning in Extensive-Form Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the minimax regret of full-information online decision making in extensive-form games. For prediction with expert advice, the optimal regret is $Θ(\sqrt{T\log K})$, where $K$ is the number of experts, or equivalently, the number of normal-form actions. For treeplex strategy spaces, existing efficient algorithms, including KOMWU and online mirror descent with the weight-one dilated entropy regularizer, achieve regret $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{V}|})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of reduced normal-form strategies. We prove that this logarithmic dependence is minimax optimal in the worst-case full-information reward model. The main difficulty is that pure plans in a treeplex are not independent experts: their rewards are correlated through the recursive structure of decisions and observations. To capture this correlation, we introduce tropical Gaussian formulae, recursive Gaussian expressions built from maxima and normalized sums which preserve the variance. The index count of such a formula matches the number of reduced normal-form continuation plans in the corresponding subtree. Our main analytic result shows that every log-balanced tropical Gaussian formula with index count $N$ has Gaussian width $Ω(\sqrt{\log N})$. While a direct approach struggles to recover this lower bound, our proof uses a spherical entropy profile to measure scale-dependent separation among the Gaussian directions, and then applies Turán's theorem and Sudakov minoration to obtain the width lower bound. Applying this result to treeplexes gives an oblivious hard distribution with valid transition outcome and Rademacher terminal rewards, establishing a regret lower bound of $Ω(\sqrt{T\log|\mathcal{V}|})$. This matches known upper bounds up to universal constants and shows that the DilEnt/KOMWU dependence on the reduced normal-form complexity is unavoidable.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Cycle structure of best-response dynamics in random bimatrix games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the best-response dynamics in games with random payoffs. We consider two-player bimatrix games, with $n$ strategies each. We assume that payoffs come from a continuous distribution, and study the best-response dynamics of these games, after imposing some structure on their payoff matrices. In particular, we focus on symmetric games, antisymmetric games, common-interest games, zero-sum games, and games with independent payoffs. When two players take turns in playing the best response to the opponent's action, they eventually end up cycling through the same sequence of actions. The main focus of the paper is the cycle structure of large random games. In particular, we study the number of cycles, the number of cycles of a certain length, the length of the longest cycle, and related quantities. We show that the structure of the game has an important impact on the typical cycle structure. Our arguments are based on a representation of the best-response dynamics of these games as directed bipartite graphs, and on the cycle structure that arises in them.

Information Retrieval.title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
Information Retrieval.summary: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.
Information Retrieval.comment: 10 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on AI-Ready Data for Science Discovery (ADSD), IEEE ICDM 2026

Information Retrieval.title: Purin: A Biology-inspired Mechanism for Artificial Neural Networks
Information Retrieval.summary: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) usually represent neural transmission with fixed trainable weights during a training batch, which omits short-term changes in synaptic efficacy. In addition, the discrete time-step simulation requires additional temporal processing that many conventional ANN architectures do not use. To overcome these challenges, we propose Purin, a biology-inspired and ANN-compatible mechanism, that introduces synaptic efficacy modulation into conventional convolutional neural networks. Purin uses a time-interval-based abstraction for neural activities, which allows Purin to introduce short- and long-term synaptic efficacy changes without using discrete time-steps. Purin introduces a bounded factor to represent temporary synaptic efficacy changes, together with two weight matrices that represent input-side and output-side efficacy. The weight matrices are updated by backpropagation and interpreted as the long-term synaptic efficacy changes. Experimental results show that after removing the confounding factors in the AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet architectures, Purin improves the classification accuracies in all three models across the evaluated datasets.
Information Retrieval.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, 8 tables

Information Retrieval.title: Making Strides in Symbolic Imitation Learning: Offline Demonstrations, Online Tuning
Information Retrieval.summary: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods have been the dominant paradigm in continuous control tasks due to their efficacy in function approximation, while interpretable evolutionary methods have lagged largely behind for the opposite reason. In this work, we introduce Symbolic Imitation Learning, a framework for distilling an oracle policy through an offline dataset into a decision list with linear model motion primitives. We show that this, in conjunction, with online Augmented-Random Search (ARS) tuning of the constants and motion primitives approximates the performance of the oracle across 20 benchmark RL tasks and exceeds the oracle in 11 of those 20 tasks while simultaneously producing parsimonious, interpretable policies that domain experts can better understand.
Information Retrieval.comment: 16 pages + 17 pages of supplementary, 9 tables, 7 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Toward Controlling Biology with Language: Offline Learning of Prompt-Conditioned Interventions for Cells, Organoids, and Biobots
Information Retrieval.summary: Natural language has become an interface to code, images and molecules, but not to living matter: a stimulus applied to cells has no fixed linguistic meaning, and every paired example of an instruction and its outcome costs a wet-lab experiment. We ask how far an existing archive of experiments can take this interface, using xenobots, motile multicellular constructs made of frog cells, stimulated by a single electrical pulse of varying duration. We re-track 155 archived recordings with two independent methods, measure what the pulse does from each bot's own behaviour before and after it, and separate behaviours the pulse controls from behaviours it does not. Longer pulses stop bots and short pulses leave them moving, sometimes faster; turning direction and starting from rest do not depend on duration, and restarting at most weakly. We then replace hand-made behaviour labels with a blind language critic: fresh sessions of a multimodal language model read plots of each bot and score how well its behaviour matches each of 176 instructions. The critic agrees with the measured labels whenever its plots contain the information the labels are defined on, and dose curves learned from its scores match those learned from the measurements. A prompt-to-intervention model trained only on critic scores maps unseen instructions, including negations, to the right end of the dose range on unseen bots, as well as the same model trained on measured labels. The archive therefore supports a calibrated, refusing language interface for the three behaviours a pulse can set, and identifies, rather than hides, the behaviours it cannot.
Information Retrieval.comment: 18 pages, 9 figures. v2: full reanalysis. Archive re-tracked with two independent trackers; measured outcomes for eight behaviours; blind language critic validated against measurements; prompt-to-intervention model outputs a dose-response curve and is evaluated on unseen instructions and unseen bots

Information Retrieval.title: Representing the Non-dominated Set of Multi-objective Network Problems by Supported Non-dominated Points
Information Retrieval.summary: In multi-objective combinatorial optimization, unsupported non-dominated points typically outnumber supported points and are often significantly more challenging to compute. Recent studies show that extreme supported non-dominated points provide high-quality representations of the non-dominated set for certain binary problems. We demonstrate that this observation does not generalize to capacitated network optimization problems: representation quality decreases with increasing arc capacities, whereas supported non-dominated points consistently provide high-quality representations with respect to several quality indicators. However, supported point sets may still be too large in practical applications, where only a small, fixed number of alternatives is typically desired. Selecting fixed-size representations from the non-dominated set requires its computationally expensive generation and thus diminishes the computational advantages that representations are intended to provide. We therefore suggest the (extreme) supported points as alternative candidate sets in subset selection problems. Our numerical results show that restricting the candidate set to supported non-dominated points yields fixed-size representations of nearly the same quality as those selected from the complete non-dominated set. Overall, supported non-dominated points serve both as high-quality representations and as reasonable candidate sets for subset selection.

Information Retrieval.title: Design and Analysis of Temporal Representations in Neural Networks
Information Retrieval.summary: Neural networks, spiking or not, compute with amplitudes: activation values, spike counts, firing rates, never event times. No measure exists of how much a network uses time. We propose one, the degree of temporal representation: the fraction of a network's four functions (encoding, activation, decoding, learning) whose variables or parameters are temporal, and hypothesise that it predicts performance on temporal tasks. At fixed architecture, accuracy and energy efficiency increase with the degree: a delay network of maximal degree reaches 98.94\% on Google Speech Commands with 175k parameters, above transformers. To test whether networks of different degree really differ, we convert the delay network into artificial and spiking networks with the same inputs and outputs. From this common start, the artificial one learns differently and temporal gradients depend on event times. Hence we obtain a design rule: for temporal data, make event times variables of a network's functions. Spiking networks, converted after training, keep the delay network's accuracy, unreachable by spiking networks trained from scratch.

Information Retrieval.title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
Information Retrieval.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, event-driven computation on neuromorphic hardware, where response time, or latency, matters as much as energy for real-time applications. Time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding with learnable synaptic delays is a natural way to exploit the timing of events. However, in state-of-the-art spiking neuron models, spike times emerge from nonlinear membrane dynamics and thresholds: no closed-form expression links network parameters to spike times, so latency can only be measured empirically, not specified or guaranteed at design time. Moreover, TTFS models are mostly evaluated on static datasets, which hides their latency on truly temporal data. Our hypothesis is that, if spike times are computed directly as closed-form functions of presynaptic spike times and synaptic delays, bypassing membrane potential and thresholding, latency becomes an explicit function of the learnable parameters that can be bounded, and therefore controlled, analytically. We build on this hypothesis with the Delay Neural Network (DeNN) in real time, which turns event streams into successive single-spike images, computes each spike time from standardised inter-spike intervals and synaptic delays, and links successive images through a long-term memory. We prove lower and upper bounds on the latency of every neuron of a layer, and show that bounding the synaptic parameters after training with a single hyperparameter places the latency anywhere between these bounds, without retraining. On a ten-class subset of the Google Speech Commands dataset, this post-training control exposes the accuracy--latency trade-off: a three-hidden-layer network reaches 94.25\% accuracy while deciding, on average, 477~ms after the end of the one-second input, and about 250~ms with confidence-based early decisions. Learning is also shown to concentrate the long-term memory on a few neurons. Latency thus becomes a design parameter of spiking models rather than a quantity measured after the fact, a step towards neuromorphic systems with real-time guarantees.

Information Retrieval.title: Pricing Symbolic Rules by What GNNs Leave Unlearned
Information Retrieval.summary: Symbolic knowledge (motif counts, ring counts, label constraints) is routinely added to graph neural networks (GNNs) and justified by their limited expressivity. We replace this yardstick with an exact one. The largest log-loss reduction a rule $S$ can give a model family is $I(Y;S\midσ)$ given what the family computes; every realised gain splits exactly into this term plus repaid neural debt; and for a trained network with representation $T$ the value is $I(Y;S\mid T)$, the label information training failed to extract. Rule design thus becomes rule discovery: we score candidates on the network's out-of-fold residual against calibrated permutation nulls with family-wise error control. On ZINC, discovery recovers the hidden ring term $\max(0,\ell_{\max}-6)$ of the target in three independent runs ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.001$) and beats expert cycle counts; frozen and applied to five unseen datasets it is never significantly worse than the plain network or the expert rule, and on BBBP it significantly beats both.
Information Retrieval.comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables. Accepted at the GraphML Workshop (Graph Machine Learning: Foundations, Frontiers, and Applications) at the 18th Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML 2026), Melbourne, Australia

Information Retrieval.title: Maximizing Detection Probability in UAV Search Missions using Random-Key Optimizers
Information Retrieval.summary: This paper focuses on the stochastic and real-time constraints of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) path planning in Search and Rescue (SAR) missions. We introduce a configurable data-driven and intelligent routing architecture that combines a closed-loop probability update with the Random-Key Optimizers (RKO). Our problem is mathematically modeled as a dynamic probabilistic variant of the Open Vehicle Routing Problem (OVRP), enabling the solver to switch adaptively between two objectives, thereby balancing probability maximization and resource minimization. The framework degrades elegantly under noisy priors but not under biased ones: a systematically biased map performs about half as well as flying with no prior at all. Computational tests show that the proposed scheme is scalable and competitive with single-path scenarios in terms of solution performance and serves as a strong decision guide for intelligent planning in SAR operations in unstable environments
Information Retrieval.comment: 21 pages, 3 figures

Information Retrieval.title: A method to automatically discover symbolic local learning rules
Information Retrieval.summary: We present a general method for discovering symbolic local learning rules that can replace backpropagation, applicable, in principle, to any deep learning architecture and task. The method automatically discovers local loss functions specific to each layer by (1) constructing a dictionary of monomials of local tensor variables, inspired by Penrose diagram notation, (2) regressing over coefficients weighting these monomials to build layerwise polynomial losses whose gradients together minimize a target global loss. We test the method on classification, reconstruction, and self-supervised learning tasks with small multilayer networks and minimal datasets. Across all tasks, the discovered rules induce non-trivial interactions between layers, which lead to significant reductions in the corresponding global losses. Furthermore, the method selects sparse combinations of monomials, finding local rules that are more interpretable than those generated by MLP-based alternatives. The potential implications of our method range from energy-efficient deep learning to the discovery of biologically plausible learning mechanisms.

Information Retrieval.title: AscendMOEA: An Ascend NPU-Accelerated Platform for Tensorized Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms
Information Retrieval.summary: Multi-objective evolutionary optimization increasingly involves large populations, expensive problem evaluations, and diverse algorithmic structures. These workloads expose the limited parallelism of loop-based implementations, while rewrites for accelerator execution can alter selection order, tie handling, and population updates. AscendMOEA is presented as a scalable platform that executes multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) on Huawei Ascend neural processing units (NPUs) and conventional central processing units (CPUs). The platform represents the decision vectors, objectives, constraints, and auxiliary states as tensors and provides reusable interfaces for algorithms, problems, population operators, quality indicators, monitoring, and repeated experiments. Dense computations are executed in batches, such as dominance, distance, variation, and problem-evaluation calculations. Short recurrences with causal dependencies retain their prescribed order and consume precomputed tensor results, which preserves the behavior of the original algorithms. AscendMOEA contains 18 algorithms, 155 benchmark and application problems, 19 public operator interfaces, and 11 quality indicators. Experiments on eight Ascend NPUs and 192 physical CPU cores evaluate operator throughput, end-to-end runtime, memory consumption, numerical agreement, and implementation ablation. Tensorized operators obtain a median acceleration of 1.58 times on the NPU. At large population scales, complete algorithms achieve a median acceleration of 5.76 times while retaining the recorded quality indicators. Moreover, the results identify the workload scale and ordered computation that determine whether accelerator execution is beneficial. AscendMOEA is open-sourced at https://github.com/dqlme/AscendMOEA.

Information Retrieval.title: Attention Is Only as Good as Its Witnesses: When Higher-Order Layers Help, and When They Do Not
Information Retrieval.summary: Transformers stop learning graph search as graphs grow, and learn the card game SET only after many distinct questions, although attention can represent both. We read these failures, and the uneven record of higher-order attention, from what a layer sums over: each layer we study computes the partition function of a family of witnesses and reads it at a temperature. Two laws follow. The depth law is a known result of logic, which we state for these layers: L layers over two-step walks reach exactly 2^L - 1 steps, just as a logical statement with L nested clauses of the form "there is a vertex such that" sees exactly that far. We build a construction that reaches this far, checked in Lean, and, when vertices carry no names, no such network reaches further. The size law is the cost of reading at a temperature, which logic does not have: existence is read correctly at every size, in the worst case, if and only if inverse temperature times margin is at least the logarithm of the number of candidates. Layers built on these laws, and on two principles that we test, learn where Transformers fail. One propagator layer trained on 49-vertex graphs answers every question at every search depth on 250-vertex graphs. Given the modulus 3, exponential Newton computes the softmax of 2-simplicial attention over pairs exactly in 3^d n operations for d clocks; with six clocks it learns SET from as few deals as 2-simplicial attention and transfers from 8- to 20-card tables. On CLRS-30 without hints, a 186,000-parameter block of OR-join and power-mean channels matches (within half a point) or beats a model of at least 73 million parameters on 9 of 12 graph tasks of the official test set, and on 8 of 12 with freshly drawn test graphs. The same account explains where pair layers did not help and where parallel layers must loop.
